newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana at 40, could be better, nationalists say.
newsitem.headline: Ghana at 40, could be better, nationalists say.

text.p: Fireworks heralded Ghana's 40th birthday on Thursday, but for veterans of a nationalist struggle against British rule, there seemed to be little to celebrate.
"I feel bitterness because the people are suffering," said Kojo Botsio, 81, who was the most important aide to reverred late founding president Kwame Nkrummah.
"There is so much hardship now. And we are not making any progress," Botsio told Reuters.

"This is not the Ghana I expected 40 years ago. I expected much better conditions of living because we had planned to develop industry and agriculture. Instead we are living more on trading than on producing," added the former education minister.
Botsio cited political instability as the main reason why Ghana -- the Black Star of Africa -- failed to live up to its promise of greatness after its comparatively early independence.
But Nkrumah's former finance minister, Komla Gbedema, blames his socialist boss's CHOICE OF Marxist-style central planning.

"Economic development was not properly planned. And things started collapsing as early as 1960 when Nkrumah took full control of finance and economy," said Gbedemah, who was sidelined and dismissed the following year.
Nkrumah's turn came five years later when he was toppled by the military in the first of a seris of six coups.
Nine years after independence Ghanaians danced in the streets once more, this time celebrating their liberation from Nkrummah's repressive policies and financial mismanagement.

"Nkrumah has been a big asset and a big disaster for the country. Politically and culturally he was the greatest African of our century. All African nationalist leaders were inspired by him," historian and politician Albert Adu Boahen told Reuters.

"Economically Nkrumah was a disaster for Ghana and for the continent. In the first two decades most countries followed his ideas of one-party system and a Marxist-Leninist approach of development," said Boahen.

"This could have been a land flowing with milk and honey. Before independence Ghana was more advanced than Malaysia and Singapore. Now the Malaysians come here to buy up our state-owned enterprises," he said.
Malaysian firms this year bought up core stakes in Ghana's national telephone company, the top commercial bank, a shipyard, and the film industry.

But Botsio still counts some benefits of independence despite his own travails in the 1970s -- he was sentenced to death over a failed 1973 coup but this was commuted to life and he was freed in 1977.

"No, I do not regret independence. Without independence many things couldn't have been done for Ghana. Like having an airline, universities, and a dam for electricity generation. They (the British) would have never allowed it," said Botsio.

Nkrumah died in exile in 1972. In 1992 Ghana's current President Jerry Rawlings ordered his body to be reburied in a mausoleum-cum-museum built on the very spot where he declared independence on March 6, 1957 on the old Polo Grounds in Accra.
"I am an Nkrumaist but Nkrumah made certain errors," said former ambassador Kofi Awoonor, 61, a key Rawlings aide.
He said it took some time for Rawlings, who has ruled for 15 years, to appreciate what Nkrummah did. Now Rawlings was bestowing due honour on Nkrummah while correcting his errors.
He cited increased and liberalised air traffic, press freedom resulting in a proliferation of newspapers, radio stations and, soon, commercial television stations.

"These are signs that we are moving somewhere. I still wished we were richer, more productive. We still have this endemic poverty. The bureaucracy is not on the ball, there is misuse of financial resources," Awoonor added.
